items.title: "Papa Jack" Laine and Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine Interview, 1960-05-23
items.q: And I stuck it in Chink's hand. I said, whether you know or not, I said, you're going to learn this thing.

ctx.x: What about Chinka Martin? He's living. He's living. He's living. Oh yeah. He played with you in the old days.

Oh yeah. Here's a queer thing. This is a really coincidence. Yeah, it seems. I had a man by the name of Kaskrow playing bass with me, you know. And he took very sick. And that takes me one of them Wild West show jobs. And I needed a tuba player. See? So Kaskrow couldn't play. He was sick. Down and out couldn't play. So I borrowed the horn from him. See? Yeah. And I stuck it in Chink's hand. I said, whether you know or not, I said, you're going to learn this thing. Yes or no? For me? You're going to learn it? He…
Oh, yes. One of those. One of the guys.

items.title: Chink Martin Interview, 1966-10-19
items.q: Jack Lane gave me the name of Chink Morton.

ctx.x: Yeah. What was your first instrument then? A guitar or a mandolin?

No, the guitar was my first instrument. The guitar was the very first. Yeah. I had one of the best professors, in fact. Well, that was years ago. You might remember, I don't forgot it was in what city it was, but the Queen's own band from Spain, New Mexico came down here. And he happened to be the baritone player, the brass baritone player. Baritone player. And he was a guitarist. When I say he was a guitarist, he was one of the finest, like that. Well, when the band went back, he stood here. What was his name?…
Not around chargers and Ursulines anyhow.

items.title: "Papa Jack" Laine, Mrs. "Papa Jack" Laine and Johnny Wiggs Interview, 1959-02-27
items.q: Put the tuba in the Chinaman's hand. Every night we played for two weeks.

ctx.x: All right, he said. If you say so, it's all right. We stood by number nine, Jane Jane House, on Decatur and Espinade. I lined them all around the circle. Said to the Chinaman, I said, whenever you can catch time, the Chinaman, that you can fill up a note, put it in there. This baritone, I said, hold up as much as possible for you. All right. Put the tuba in the Chinaman's hand. Every night we played for two weeks. Every night for two weeks. Chinaman on the tube. Start to put them in parades. Start to moat around.…

items.title: "Papa Jack" Laine Interview, 1964-04-25
items.q: Well a friend of mine, I thought of the Chinaman, Martin. I runs up to Casco and I borrow his tuba. And I give the tuba to this boy to play.

ctx.x: Yeah. You were going to tell us about the Wild West show?

Yes. Well, this is a coincidence that happened to me. I had a man, young man, playing tuba. His name was Joe Cascaro. And one day he took seriously sick. Now that evening he sent me word that he wasn't able to come down to play music with me and play us at this Wild West showcase. Well here I wasn't a terrible fix. Well a friend of mine, I thought of the Chinaman, Martin. I runs up to Casco and I borrow his tuba. And I give the tuba to this boy to play. He said to me, I don't know nothing about... I said you…
This was a marching band? Marching band? Marching band. Marching band.
